utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We lost some time this morning, and this is how we plan to make up the time: Mr. Milosevic to spend another hour, to 10.45 in examination-in-chief -- sorry, yes. Mr. Milosevic, another hour, to 10.20. And we take the first break at -- we take the break at 10.45, and with the indulgence of the interpreters, for five minutes -- for ten minutes, resuming at 10.55, and working until ten past twelve when we will have to break to allow for the changeover for the Appeals Chamber. Mr. Milosevic. KOSTA MIHAILOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off at Fred Singleton's paper. The title of its paper and especially its content lead to the conclusion that the increase in development in Slovenia and Croatia, on the one hand, he saw as the main reason of political tensions in Yugoslavia. This is what follows from the article. In connection with this, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Professor Singleton saw perfectly clearly what the regional situation was in Yugoslavia and that he identified the issues quite rightly; the deepening of differences in development between Slovenia and Croatia on the one hand and the rest of Yugoslavia on the other hand. This was almost obvious, and it was not hard to establish this, especially, of course, if somebody wished to see what the real situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As proof of his thesis that economic relations had a decisive influence on interethnic or international tensions, he points out that the mass movement in Croatia and the demonstrations of 1971 was important. Something very strange happened: The students demanded a change in the foreign currency regime. Please look at page 293 of his paper, where he says: "The figures show that both Croatia and Slovenia [In English] [Previous translation continues]... last 25 years steadily improved, both in absolute per capita income and also their relative income in comparison with the less-developed republics." [Interpretation] He goes on: "[In English] [Previous translation continues]... what has been taken from the wealthier republics then to assess the benefits they have received from the cheap food and raw materials and more recently the cheap, unskilled labour which they have been able to import from the poorer regions." [Interpretation] In connection with what I asked you, and I ask you to comment on this, on page 294, in his paper, in tab 7, he says: "It is interesting to note [In English] [Previous translation continues]... that the students who protested in the streets of Zagreb in November 1971 used to slogans such as 'End the plunder of Croatia,' and 'Foreign exchange resources to those who earn' them. Foreign exchange resources --" [Interpretation] Foreign exchange sources. "[In English] [Previous translation continues]... those who earn them, those who really --" [Interpretation] These were the slogans. He goes on, and I quote -- he goes on to say that the then president of the party in Croatia, Savka Davcevic-Kucar, spoke "[In English] [Previous translation continues]... Socialist Sovereign State of Croatia within the framework of Socialist Yugoslavia which is a national state of the Croat nation." [Interpretation] Do you see in this a correct description of the growth in tensions and what caused them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this example that you gave of the student demonstrations, which came out with slogans about the lack of hard currency to the detriment of Croatia, I think that this is pure ideology, nationalist ideology within the mass movement that took place in Croatia. From what was said yesterday and today, we have seen that Croatia was a republic with above average development and pulling a detail out of context could not be justified. Also, it is not true in itself, because Croatia insisted on the -- on using more foreign exchange because it was the exporter of final products. It did not, however, take into account the input coming from other republics; for example, electric power, raw materials such as copper and lead, labour, and so on and so forth, and this was met with severe criticism by economists who saw this demand as totally unjustified. It's interesting to note that this did yield some results, because in spite of these demonstrations which were nationalist and which had to be condemned even in Croatia itself, Croatia did obtain an increase in the quota of foreign exchange remaining at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. What was Tito's attitude to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't object to that question, but I shouldn't like it to be thought that it's concession that this is an appropriate way of using somebody else's writings and opinions. It doesn't seem to me from my understanding of the question and of the document of Singleton that he's an eyewitness. Now, it's one thing to ask a witness to comment on what's in somebody else's report reflecting eyewitness evidence. It's entirely another thing to simply put before a witness an article of someone else and then to try and get the article in and to try and get comment based on it. It seems to me we are entering a difficult area, and I would ask the Chamber to limit the accused in his use of other materials to the same parameters that applied to us. Before I sit down, this of course, an expert is entitled to and typically does cite authorities. So he might cite in a footnote Singleton, something like that. If not cross-examined on the point, then the document will typically not go in. If cross-examined on it, then typically it may go in. That seems to me the normal practice we've been following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. We take account of the point that you have made. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, gentlemen, that you have in mind that these assessments by an expert such as Fred Singleton are fully in accordance with the assessments made by Professor Mihailovic. So that from the viewpoint of an economist from Yugoslavia and from the viewpoint of a foreign observer who was also highly competent, we see that they say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you know Fred Singleton personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I once met him while he was studying in Belgrade, and we had a long conversation, but this was after he wrote his article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even this meeting of yours could not affect what he wrote in this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he represented the situation objectively, as far as I can see. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the attitude of Tito towards the Croatian mass movement, the nationalist wave in the '70s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was ambivalent. Professor Singleton established that Tito acted decisively, but this is true only at one point in time. This was a very bizarre situation. In the summer of 1971, manoeuvres were held on the -- and on the 16th of September, when the manoeuvres ended, there was a reception in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Hotel Esplanade. Tito welcomed the party chief from Croatia, Savka Davcevic-Kucar, and he toured Croatia and learned precisely what was going on in Croatia, that all kinds of things were being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've just stopped you because you have already answered the question that Mr. Milosevic asked. You said his attitude was ambivalent. We don't have much time. Move on to another question, We don't have much time. Move on to another question, please, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to say that in tab 14 and tab 15, you have reports from that time, from the leading newspaper Politika, and I will quote only a small part where Tito says, that was on Tuesday the 9th of May, 1972, and the article is entitled what Tito Told The Croatian Leadership Last Summer, and it says that the demons of nationalism are gathering under the wing of nationalism, all kinds of opposing opinions, and so on and so forth. And then he goes on to say that the situation in Croatia is not good, that Croatia has become a key problem in the country because of rampant nationalism. Tito, the unchallenged leader of the country at the time, said that Croatia had become a key problem because of rampant nationalism. And then in tab 15, you have what Professor Mihailovic now said. He said that I -- "This time I saw that there are some really absurd stories about Croatia, that a lot of chauvinism exists and flourishes there. This is incorrect." And this was followed by applause. Does this, Professor, express what you just said, his ambivalent attitude? I wouldn't even use the word ambivalent; I would call it two-faced. Is this a two-faced attitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, did Tito actually support Croatian nationalism at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what follows from his statement. Maybe he felt personally threatened because he had a young and aggressive political team which was probably threatening his personal position. And this could have been a reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on a bit faster. What was the response of the party in Serbia? You were then a member of the administration of the Literary Association.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the principle of symmetry, nationalism had to be discovered and pointed out in the other republics, and they wanted to find a counterpart to the Croatian nationalism in Serbia. However, I think that this attempt by the Serbian party to discover nationalism, especially in the Serbian Literary Association, was unsuccessful. In Serbia -- or, rather, in Croatia it was the Matica Hrvatska that was the brain of this movement. So the counterpart in Serbia would have been the Literary Association. However, they were unable to discover any nationalist activities in that institution. In Serbia, there were only isolated and trivial and unimportant responses to that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. There was a party commission at that time which attempted to find nationalism in the Serb Literary Association at any cost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a three-member commission: Milan Milutinovic, Professor Kaparovic, and Bakocevic were its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, tell me, was there any direct or indirect recognition by the official bodies in Croatia that the Yugoslav republic -- this Yugoslav republic had above-average economic development? In pages 58 and 59 or -- in your version, and 47, 48 in the English version, speak about the improvement of the economy in Croatia. The negotiations about secession showed this because the Croatian delegation suggested that the principle of justice in division of the assets of the former SFRY had to redress the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is too fast for the interpreters to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are complaining about your speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters have Professor Mihailovic's paper, and they can read from the English translation. I assume this is not too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt, then, that this confirms that even they admitted that Croatia's development had been above average. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a bizarre detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this fact was established, is it not beyond doubt, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was surprising that they themselves put forward such a proposal, and the Yugoslav side accepted this immediately, to their surprise. When they got home and realised how well Croatia had done, they gave up their own convictions and even the principle of justice, which was to have been the foundation of any agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what were the causes and the differences in development between Croatia and the other republics and provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the territorial distribution of assets. Croatia and Slovenia, especially Slovenia, had above-average investment and a very favourable structure of investments. Also, there was the institutional system which provided conditions of exchange. There was customs protection, there was the pricing system, there were subsidies for exports, and these were all measures favouring the more developed republics. What came from the more developed republics, what they gave for the development of the less developed republics was seen only as compensation for this. If that is so, then these measures were neutralised, in a way, and investments were used to their fullest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What assets were recruited, and what was done to prevent the deepening of this gap between the more developed and less developed areas of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the measures of the development policy were very meager in Yugoslavia. There was a fund for the development of underdeveloped areas, and the contributions were between 1.50 and 1.70 of the social sector of the economy, and transfer was made to the underdeveloped areas in a very strange way. There were keys according to which funds were allocated to the underdeveloped areas. These areas authorised certain banks in their areas, and this was done automatically. Afterwards, attempts were made for those areas giving funds to this fund to take a direct part in the allocation of these resources and investments, but this was not done. The technical assistance which is normal under such circumstances was very meager. The underdeveloped areas were given the possibility of doing whatever they wanted with their means, even to use them for purposes other than those intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now let's take a look at tab 18 where we have just one part of the declaration made by the federal parliament, which was published as an official declaration of the parliament in the Official Gazette which publishes laws, bylaws, official documents of the federal parliament, generally speaking. And I'd just like to quote point 1.2, which is contained in tab 18. On the left-hand side of the column, where it says: "In keeping with the options from the long-term programme for economic stabilisation and stopping the relative lag in development in the economic development of the territory of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, outside the territories of the autonomous provinces in comparison to the overall country will be done by reliance on one's own forces, the association of labour and resources and the undertaking concrete measures of economic and developmental policy." Now, Professor, is this a clearly stated position according to which the supreme authority in Yugoslavia at that point in time takes clear note of the lag in development of the territory of Serbia outside Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the provinces and that it is intending to apply some sort of - how shall I put this? - launch a principled appeal to rely on their own forces to improve the situation whereas there were no concrete measures and steps actually taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your observation is correct. The Republic of Serbia and Serbia proper, which despite the fact that it was constantly below the Yugoslav average in terms of per capita income and per capita social product was, from the beginning, ranked as a developed area, like Slovenia and Croatia, for example. So that the sources were allocated from one fund to another, but actually this territory received nothing from the fund which in time led to a serious lagging behind in development. And it was a typical area which did not see constant development. It continued to be below average and was never able to reach that average, which meant that it was not able to see any capital accumulation and development. And on the basis of the analyses that were compiled in all the institutes of economics, there were three institutes for Yugoslav as a whole for conducting these economic analyses, and they resulted in two five-year plans, development plans, in the 1980s, and Serbia proper was not exempt from their obligations to allocate resources. But an attempt was made through six or seven different measures that were set out and taken to stop that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we don't need that much detail. We just need the main points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the economic position of Serbia, which is confirmed and borne out by the observations made by the top organs of power and authority was below the Yugoslav average; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's go back to the question once again of whether Serbia dominated or whether it did not dominate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the analyses that we have before us here, the social product of Serbia per capita decreased to 80 per cent, which means that it lagged behind approximately 20 per cent. It was 20 per cent not below the Yugoslav average but in relation to the average in the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this aspect of his evidence has been made very, very clear, that Serbia lagged behind the other republics. I think you should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, Professor, please, what were the limiting factors in Kosovo's development? Let's focus our attention now on the question of Kosovo. What were the limiting or restricting factors of Kosovo's development, and how far was economic development efficacious in comparison with the efficaciousness in the other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was very low effectiveness. There was low investment, low labour productivity, and so forth, so that in addition to the high birth rate of the population, this was one of the main causes for the area's slow development. For example, Kosovo had a rate of development in the entire post-war period of 4 per cent, looking at the overall social product development, which makes it 1.6 per cent per capita. So the demographic investments accounted for 2.4 per cent. And if to that we add the low efficiency of the investments and low labour productivity, then of course it lagged behind considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far did the federation and the Republic of Serbia itself involve itself in the financing of Kosovo? What did they do to finance Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Indirectly speaking, through the fund for the lesser developed regions, Serbia made its contributions, although Serbia also gained with Kosovo, because Kosovo increased its share annually, so ultimately used 50 per cent of the overall resources in the fund for assistance to the developing regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You studied not only the history of the population of Serbia but migrations within Yugoslavia and the economic emigration to other countries, to third countries. So what were these migrations motivated by? What caused them amongst the Yugoslav republics and within Yugoslavia, let's take that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have two motives, the economic and ethnocentric, as we call it. The economic migration was relatively smaller in scope and of lesser importance, and it occurred mostly between Slovenia and Croatia as the republics which were immigration republics and had a need for labour force coming in from other areas. They needed a labour force coming in. But what is characteristic and interesting to note as far as relationships go is the ethnocentric migration, as it was called, which went toward Serbia. And as Serbia was lagging behind, it had unemployment rate that was above average but it had this ethnocentric emigration and people coming in from Croatia and Kosovo and Slovenia which was quite unusual. If was very unusual to have a majority nation, for example, prompted by non-economic measures, to leave their homes through -- for non-economic reasons and move elsewhere, migrate elsewhere, to areas -- from areas where they had been living for centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were these Serbs from Croatia, Kosovo, and Slovenia migrating to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Into Serbia. Into Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, so that this should not be understood in a one-sided manner, you spoke about ethnocentrism as a concept and as a reason and that there was population migration and movement whereby certain nationalities from one republic would go to their central republics. And as far as I understood you, that was a general phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was a phenomenon that was evident in Bosnia, for example, because the Serbs went towards Serbia, the Croats went towards Croatia, and the Muslims, not only did they not go away, but from Serbia, from Sandzak, they would move into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what was the main reason for the Serbs leaving Kosovo, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the reason the Serbs left Kosovo, the main reason for that, was the pressure that was exerted on them. The Serbian Academy of Sciences in 1985 organised a survey organised by two university professors. They were not members of the academy themselves. Their names were Marina Blagojevic and Ruza Petrovic, and they published a report numbering 280 pages which showed all the modalities of pressure, all the ways in which pressure was exerted on the Serbs to leave, and I think that that has been attached to the documents that you already have. And that 1985 survey would be among those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, tell me, Professor, what do you think about the thesis that by the 1974 constitution the -- that Serbia abolished the autonomy of the provinces and returned the system to the system of centralisation in the whole of Yugoslavia whereas Croatia and Slovenia came out in favour of confederation and allegedly showed that they were in favour of the development of democracy? What do you think about that idea, that concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that autonomy was never abolished. That's my first point. The situation that was created through the 1974 constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must have missed it but I'm not sure that this has been covered in his expert report, has it? And what expertise does he have? And I haven't interrupted but the questions are pretty well at large and without any reference to his either source material or his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that point is well taken. Move on to another point. It's not part of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speakers make pauses between question and answer, thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must make pauses, and Professor, between question and answer in the interests of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you were one of the authors of the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. We're going to go over several questions having to do with the memorandum. Our time is limited, of course, so we'll have to be quick. Tell us when and where it was decided to write the memorandum in the first place. Was that an autonomous decision made by the Serbian Academy or did anybody influence that decision-making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a completely autonomous decision by the academy, mostly people of the social sciences, and there were several of us. Academician Maksimovic, at the Assembly held in 1985, for example, put forward the proposal according to which the establishment should be presented with a memorandum stating the seriousness of the crisis that had come upon us and that serious steps should be taken to deal with it. This was adopted in 1985, and it was almost realised in 1986 because it was never actually completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what were the reasons, the motives behind writing the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The motives were first and foremost a feeling that existed that -- of the country having entered a serious crisis and that no way out was immediately visible. And the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences not only as a science institution but as a national institution as well was deeply concerned by that. It felt that it could not keep quiet, could not keep silent, but had to state its views and present its ideas. Also, there were many scientific meetings organised by the academy that had been held beforehand in which the powers that be, the political powers that be showed themselves to be unmoved by the situation they were facing. So we felt that there should be a document which would more immediately send out a warning, an alarm to the government of the seriousness of the situation in hand. So those were the main motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After you had taken the decision to write the memorandum or, rather, the academy, as far as I know, a commission was set up numbering 16 members, members of the academy, who were supposed to put that decision into practice. You yourself were one of those members. What issues and questions did you deal with before you actually sat down to write the memorandum itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we wrote the memorandum, we discussed who the memorandum should be addressed to, where to send it out to, and then it was said that it should be addressed either to the Presidency of Serbia or the Assembly. So it was a document prepared in order to be closed from the public. I saw some versions; on one it said the Presidency of Serbia, on the other it said the Assembly of Serbia. So that's one point. Now, we discussed whether it should be a sort of programme document, setting out a programme, or a document of warning, stating that the situation was very serious and that steps should be taken. So although there were ideas put forward according to which the memorandum should contain some elements of a specific programme to deal with the situation, that was rejected. And the working group and the commission unanimously decided that it should be a strictly internal document and that if a programme was to be devised, that this should be done later on, and that's what happened. In the 1990s, or in 1990, an attempt was made to make a different -- write a different document which could resemble a national programme. However, that attempt did not succeed. We came across some misunderstandings. So these two documents are essentially different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a synopsis according -- for the document, and have you -- do you have the synopsis? Because as far as I understand it, it was preserved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a four-page synopsis setting out the basic schematic for the document and some basic theses were put forward as well. The memorandum was not original, in fact. It is a synthesis of existing knowledge and information. So in the synopsis itself, we could see basic ideas and concepts and theses being put forward. So that the synopsis itself was a synthetic picture of what was developed in the memorandum itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, how does the synopsis explain the writing of the memorandum, the causes for writing it or reasons for writing it? How is the position of Serbia defined? What is being requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the synopsis itself, as in the memorandum, we insisted upon equality, having Serbia on -- be on an equal footing in the political sense and in other senses. Nothing more than that was required. Equality. And it was also mentioned that that might not be in keeping with Serbia's position or, rather, that Serbia was historically predestined to unite that portion of the population in the Balkans and that it would have compromised its historical role had it asked for anything more than full equality with other nations, to be on a footing of equality with all the other nations and nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've said a moment ago that the memorandum was a synthesis of the scientific research already conducted. So can I take it, then, that the scientific basis for the memorandum was not any separate research worked out for the purposes of the memorandum but that the group of academicians drafting the memorandum used research that had already been conducted up until then and that it represented a synthesis of what science had established up until that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And this synthesis -- and what is important here, I would like to note this, that there was an anticipatory note of events that might take place unless steps were taken. So it was a forecast of what might happen given the crisis unless certain steps and measures were taken to deal with it. So I think that the value of that document lies therein. It anticipated what might happen. It looked at where development might lead. And it also mentioned the possibility of Yugoslavia's disintegration and breakdown, and so it confirmed that the analyses and basic foundations leading to that conclusion were sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, in view of the fact that the memorandum is said to have overly stressed the economic lagging behind of Serbia, as an economist, to what extent can you respond to such criticisms? Did the memorandum overstate the economic backwardness of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could not be either overestimated or underestimated. If Serbia was truly falling behind according to its GDP, the value of its funds, if instead of maintaining its position at a little below average or rising to average, if it was falling lower and lower below average, according to all the indications, I don't know if that was cause for equanimity or whether something had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the attacks on the memorandum, its content has often been described as nationalist. It's been characterised as a nationalistic document. Are these assessments based on the text of the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the contrary. Nationalism is condemned as one of the fundamental causes of the crisis, the deformations in the economic system, and if you have patience with me I can show you ten places where there are explicit statements against nationalism. The memorandum is criticised without ever relying on the text itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have that point. If you're asked in cross-examination, you can give the references.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The text of the memorandum is here, but for the sake of saving time, I will not ask the Professor to point out all these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the memorandum is said to be a Greater Serbia programme. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've already answered this question. This has already been said. I would describe the memorandum as a document of warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if it's not a national programme or platform, how would Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond you briefly describe the memorandum, as a document of warning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: An assessment of the situation based on scholarship and a warning of what this was leading to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that measures have to be taken, nothing more than that. That was the clear framework and goal of the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you explain, in view of the fact that especially in the West, in the Western propaganda, it has been said the memorandum is responsible for stoking the fires of nationalist conflicts between the peoples of the former Yugoslavia and that it contributed to the break-up of Yugoslavia, is this based on fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You cannot find anything like this anywhere in the memorandum. Secondly, people keep forgetting that the memorandum was not addressed to the general public at all. It was a document which was supposed to have been sent to one of the leading bodies in the republic, either the Presidency or the Assembly. The fact that it was leaked and misused in order to attack the academy, that's something that the academy's not responsible for. Neither the academy nor the document can be held responsible for this. If the language used in the memorandum is quite strong, the purpose was to wake up the top leadership which was not aware of the depth and profundity of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The memorandum is very critical of the 1974 constitution which it blames for the break-up of Yugoslavia. Are those critics of the memorandum right who see in it an advocation of a return to centralisation, the positions of AVNOJ and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think that very erroneous opinions are being bandied about with respect to centralism. The former Yugoslavia was a one-party state with a hierarchical structure. It was the party that was centralised, and the leader was at the top. After the death of Tito and Kardelj, a new situation was created where the state could not simply be a place of transmission but an original organ. What sort of centralism was this? It could not be restored in the same way that it had existed up to Tito's death, because no one could become a second Tito in the former Yugoslavia or have such pretensions, especially as Yugoslavia was broken up into a polycentrist state. No one could impose this system on anyone else any longer. People who say that confederation was a prerequisite of democratisation are wrong. This is ridiculous. This was going on to its full extent, decentralisation and democratisation, and this was ridiculous. I don't know if in other countries they -- they have to become Confederate countries in order to be democratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, have you heard about the Blue Book, and are you aware of its content? Have you read it? When you were writing the memorandum, did any member of the commission read this Blue Book? In tab 3, I will quote. The document is called the Blue Book of the Presidency of Serbia. It was drawn up in March 1977, and its full title is The Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia Constitutional Position and Practice, and the proposal was neither accepted nor rejected. Three years after the constitution of 1974, the Presidency of Serbia found that such systemic solutions had negative effects. They drew up the Blue Book, but they put it under the carpet, so to say. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard and I think that others have heard of the existence of this Blue Book. It was a document under seal. After the constitution of 1974 was enacted, the Presidency of Serbia set up a commission containing -- which was composed of university professors and prominent civil servants, people from the Assembly and so on, and their task was to show what the effects the new constitution were and what problems were emerging in connection with its implementation. This Blue Book was a confidential document. It was under seal. Rumours were going around, saying that it criticised the constitution and asked for its amendment, but text itself wasn't available. You may be surprised to hear that I found this text and was able to obtain it only a few days ago. It was published in 1990 by a journalist within the framework of certain interviews, but nobody knew anything about this. I have simply scanned it, and I think that what was said about it is correct. It is about 50 printed pages long and contains a critique of the legislation and the -- what was happening, and it shows that it was the cause of a large-scale disintegration of Serbia, that the initial -- its initial shortcomings had grown into a huge problem. This was an unsuccessful document which led to the full disintegration of Serbia, which made it an ill-defined area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This -- these were the findings of the Presidency of Serbia three years after the adoption of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just add that, according to reliable information, a three-day session was held, and there was a heated discussion in the comments to the text that was printed. It says that this was neither approved nor adopted, and there was even a proposal that the document should be burned. It had been printed in only 40 copies and those who received it had to keep it strictly confidential. I was unable to obtain the minutes and the transcripts of these discretions -- discussions, but everybody knows that Kardelj was there and that he prevented and suppressed the discussion - I think "suppressed" is the right word - so that it practically petered out. And this was characteristic of life in Serbia in general at the time. All the republics thought that they could meddle in Serbia's internal affairs while Serbia never meddled in the internal affairs of others. And I think this indicates how subservient Serbia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were a university professor at the time, tell me, how did professional academic scholarly circles respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a response to the amendments which were built in as the mainstays of this constitution. At the faculty of law, there was a very strong reaction to this. Professor Mihailovic, who is now an academician, and a secretary of our department were sentenced to eight months in prison, and he served this sentence, because he was critical. He made a speech, it's five or six typewritten pages long, and I think it's in the documentation, from which it can clearly be seen that he started from the positions that nationalism and the problems of the state were issues that should not be prominent in the 21st century, especially not in our parts. However, at that time Croatian nationalism was not only aggressive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, according to the schedule that I outlined at the start of the proceedings, there are just another three or four minutes for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will put only one question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, how do you explain the large-scale propaganda campaign in the West against the memorandum of the Serb Academy of Sciences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This propaganda did not exist from the very beginning. I even think that judging by the responses of the embassies in Belgrade, it was seen as an act of civil courage, but the situation changed with the break-up of Yugoslavia. The West accepted the thesis of Serbian -- of -- interpreter's apology -- Croatian and Slovenian propaganda. This is easy to refute, but this was propagated on a wide scale. In the press, in so-called scholarly institutions, they all copied texts from each other without ever looking at the original text and never relying on an analysis of the original text of the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can imagine the circumstances where we'll be somewhat pressed for time at the end of the morning. I don't forecast asking many, if any, questions about the accused's exhibits, the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Defence exhibits. I'm concerned that we may be facing an application to let in really a large amount of documentation that hasn't either been cited or quoted from at all and has simply been identified, and in those circumstances I wonder if it might be prudent on this occasion to deal with the Defence exhibits now in order not to avoid -- in order to avoid dealing with them in a great rush at the end of the morning. I'm happy to do it either way, obviously, but I can see problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any specific opposition except for tab 19 and 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't been, I'm afraid, noting exhibits on an exhibit-by-exhibit basis because sometimes it's been going too quickly for me, but it seems to me that there's been a lot of simply identifying a document and then not referring to it or quoting from it at all. And if we are to pursue the same policy which we have been pursuing to date of dealing, in our analysis for the concluding arguments, with every document that comes in, and I suspect that the Chamber with its legal officers is doing the same thing, we are adding substantially to the burden of work without the material necessarily having any evidential value. That's my concern. There have been these very large books and I'm not sure what their status is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether in this case if you have some specific opposition to the specific exhibits, tabs, except for tab 19 and tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the very big ones. Yes, I think -- in the earlier ones -- for example, we've just looked at Klava Kniva [phoen], the Blue Book. That one is probably an exhibit that we should have in because it's part of the narrative, but it's only been referred to, it hasn't actually been quoted from. I don't mind with that case. But with all the others, I think where there's simply been reference, and I haven't identified exactly which ones it is because it has been going fast, I can't see any real reason to have them in. And there was the problem, again, about the -- the problem I raised earlier about the report or the opinion of another author which was simply borrowed. It wasn't -- it wasn't being cited for any reason except to borrow it and repeat it. It may be something the Chamber would want to think about in the short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was operating under the pressure of time. I think that's why he just made references.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just say it is a learned report with these references in these tabs plainly going to the report and the argument of this witness, which has a very clear direction when you consider the whole of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit all of the documents in the binder except for tab 19. We admit them on the basis of the references made to them. 20 is not admitted. Those that haven't been translated will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The expert report will be marked as D265, and the binder of the expert witness will be D266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a minute. Since we're dealing with exhibits, I'm reminded there are three exhibits from the last witness -- four? Four exhibits. Well, three or four, and we just want to have them admitted now. Do you have them ready? I think we're losing time. Let's continue with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next tab numbers will be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll come back to these. We'll come back to those at the end of the day's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I will deal with this witness today. I shall, therefore, have to be extremely selective in the material I put to him and won't necessarily be able to advance all aspects of our case with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long, Professor, have you known the accused personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known him since 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been not only working with him but you've become friends of his -- a friend of his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you could call it friend. I don't know how one defines friendship. He asked me to take part, in 1988, in the work of the Commission for the Economic Reform. So I cooperated with him in the commission until 1991, until the commission lasted and worked. We had about 40 meetings, 40 sessions, and our relationship was very proper. Now, whether they were -- whether it was friendship, I can't say that it was intimate friendship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also assisted him following the Karadjordjevo meeting in March of 1991, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was never in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meetings that followed the Karadjordjevo meeting, the meetings of the group of experts, did you take part in those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which group you're referring to. Could you tell me what meetings and which group of experts you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later because I want to deal with things chronologically, but thank you for your answer so far. Let's go to the memorandum. The memorandum, it is said, was leaked. Subsequently in 1995, there was an edition of the memorandum published together with Answers to Criticisms, and that document was prepared by you and Vasilije Krestic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have that as an exhibit in this case, number D250, I think. Do you have a copy of that document before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber doesn't have their copy with them I'll lay the appropriate passages on the overhead projector. Can we ask for the assistance of the usher, please, and we'll lay the -- lay this on the overhead projector, just a couple of passages to look at, partly to remind the Judges of what it contains and to look at one or two particular items.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look on what is the English page 17 - and it may be that we'll find the corresponding reference for you in the Serbian version - at the foot of page 17, we find this passage: "The unauthorised --" I'll read it to you, Professor, you will remember it, I expect. "The unauthorised version of the text which was leaked to the public had not received approval. Finally, the chapter stated its opinion that there were compelling reasons for work on this important project to be continued." The next paragraph begins: "Unfortunately, the public outcry over the memorandum did not die down even after the meeting of the party chapter." Professor, we have done an analysis which I hope was made available to you by the Defence, but it may not have been, comparing the original 1986 version, which was always said to be a draft, with the version published by you in 1995, and there were found to be only six short passages that were different between the two versions. Are you aware of the fact that the limit -- the differences between the two versions were as limited as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about those differences. The only difference I know about is that a line from the economic section was left out in the typing, omitted in the typing. There was a version that was considered and copied in a number of copies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think 20, the witness said, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and there was a collective editorship which was not completed, was edited, and 16 copies were distributed among the 16 members of the commission. Three went to those who were provisional consultants, such as Dobrica Cosic, Professor Jovan Djordjevic, and Luba Tadic, those three. And one copy remained Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond undistributed as far as my memory serves me. So 20 copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any differences between the text that was printed and published. And if there are any differences, then they can only be negligible, minor differences, not of any substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see -- thank you for that. That, then, probably confirms our analysis. The limited differences between the 1986 version and the version finally published in your Answers to Criticisms in 1995 raises as a possibility that far from being accidentally leaked, the document was intentionally leaked in 1986. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was absolutely not leaked intentionally, and it was shocking when it appeared, the article in the Vecernje Novosti newspaper. The editorial board had a meeting and they asked the question of have you -- the rest of us, Have you read the Vecernje Novosti edition? And we said, Why should we read the Vecernje Novosti? And they said, Well, look at the article. And we interrupted our meeting straight away when we heard about it. But I think how the memorandum came out is a fact that is well known. It went through Professor Jovan Djordjevic, who was sent a copy of the version with a request for his remarks and comments, and there's no doubt that it left his house, that that's where it came from, from his house. And this was confirmed by his daughter. The only question is which of the two versions is the correct version, whether his son-in-law, who was a journalist of the Vecernje Novosti newspaper, took the document on his own initiative or whether Professor Djordjevic himself gave the document to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia since he had previously cooperated with Kardelj and others and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If I can cut you short. Can we look, please, with the usher's assistance, at page 24 in the English version. In the middle of the page, please. And we found this passage in your answer to criticism: "Even though the propaganda against the Serbian Academy and memorandum was far from innocuous, the Serbian public did not allow itself to be hoodwinked. A small section of the public might let itself be taken in out of ignorance and might believe the propaganda being drummed into them, but the majority of educated citizens who had some knowledge of the contents of the memorandum realised that the accusations levelled against the Serbian Academy were unfounded and the interpretation given of its motives and messages skewed. The Serbian Academy's prestige rose rapidly in the eyes of Serbian society, for this learned institution ..." and it goes on. You see, did this memorandum serve to mobilise public opinion in a nationalist way, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I can't seem to find the text in Serbian, the passage in Serbia. As to the translation, I have a translation of the translation; I don't think you're going to have the right thing. Let me just find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It begins: "Even though the propaganda against ..." In the paragraph immediately preceding the headline Croatian Criticism of the Memorandum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this sounds a little different, so please give me time to read through it. "Even though the propaganda against," et cetera, et cetera, "against the Serbian Academy memorandum was far from innocuous, the Serbian public did not allow itself to be hoodwinked." A small section of the public might let itself be taken in out of ignorance and might believe the propaganda being drummed into them, but the majority of educated citizens who had some knowledge of the contents of the memorandum realised that the accusations levelled against the Serbian Academy were unfounded and the interpretation given of its motives and messages skewed. The Serbian Academy's prestige --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor stopped there. Perhaps you could put your question again --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- now that the Professor has read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this memorandum serve to mobilise public opinion in a nationalist way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please. This memorandum was not addressed to the public at all, and I repeated this. It was to be a closed document, so it was written with a -- with the kind of language that was supposed to animate the political establishment. It had no pretensions whatsoever of going public at all. And we had decided that. That was the decision we had taken previously by which the memorandum should be a restricted document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would help me, and if the Chamber would permit us to use, for reasons of speed, a highlighted version of an existing exhibit, Exhibit 800, the memorandum -- the chapter from the late Ivan Stambolic's book. If you would be good enough to place it on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you will know, Professor, Ivan Stambolic initiated the process that led to this memorandum, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean "initiated the process" that led to the memorandum. What do you mean by that? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll describe the passage in the way he described it himself later, but will you now please listen to what he himself in his book wrote about it. The first passage -- is that the first page you've got there? Yes, it is -- asked the question: "Were the nationalists the most dangerous opponents? He said: "They were and still are, but it's even worse that they are, objectively, enemies of the people. This is precisely why I immediately declared the memorandum as what it would become: An obituary of Yugoslavia. I do not find any satisfaction in this true prophecy." He went on to say: "The advocates of pro-memorandum Serbia first tried to subdue Yugoslavia, tightening it until bursting point. After that, after they have failed, they will go to war against it, using all of their force against the policies of the cool heads, which included mine. I was not wrong in believing that the memorandum's makers, the instigators of today's fratricide, were calling upon horrible evil." Now, here is the accused's immediate predecessor as leader of the Communist Party and a man who set up, as we've heard in evidence, this process of preparing a memorandum. Can you explain why, with his knowledge of your country, he could express those views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know what? He was on the opposite side. He initiated the campaign. And quite clearly, he is trying to defend the campaign and his steps which were quite inappropriate. You could read what Stane Kavcic said, for example, on the other hand, about the memorandum; that the politicians did not have the reason to read the -- that they did not read the document and see that it was speaking about real things and that they didn't have the strength to come into contact with the people who wrote the memorandum. So this is a defence of one's positions, a repression that was exerted. They are insinuations which just don't hold water, because he didn't initiate it. It now turns out that the memorandum created that crisis, whereas the memorandum was writing about the crisis once it had become a deep-seated crisis and once the situation had become explosive. And it issues warnings. It cautions people like Stambolic and like-minded people to the fact that they should open their eyes wide and take steps to do something about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look at the next page and the next highlighted passage. Then I think that will be all I will have time for with this document. His other observations, and the Chamber can see them all in due course, when asked, "What was your opinion about the presence of the memorandum?" he replied: "I believe that science should be more present in efforts to solve our social, economic, political and other problems. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Therefore, why should the academy, our highest institution, not join these efforts? That is why we had agreed with the academy's leadership, one year before the memorandum would appear, that it should organise several teams made up of different experts who would deal with current social issues ..." Later asked, "Hence the story that you were the one who ordered the memorandum," he relied in part: "When I read it, I clearly knew what they meant by 'helping' us in solving social and economic problems. I immediately reacted in a speech at Belgrade University in late October 1986. At that time, I said I was expecting the academicians to help carry the load that we were carrying instead of trying to trip us! I called it political insinuation which does not create science but evil blood and darkness." Were you aware of the late Ivan Stambolic making that speech, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but it is an incorrect diagnosis. It's a quite deformed, distorted vision by a politician who himself was in large measure responsible for the state of affairs. So he was speaking pro domo sua. He was speaking in defence of the policy that the memorandum was criticising. So his positions were quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is completely valueless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have a sufficient answer on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, as with all the material, I'm going to have to deal with it by sample. The remainder of the material will have to be available with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll take a break for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the usher please place on the overhead projector the English language --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the usher please place on the overhead projector the English language version of the memorandum at page 21 towards the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One last passage from the memorandum, Professor. Where we see that you and your colleague recorded the following about its history. Just from the top of the page: "The memorandum struck a chord with the public which had many of its own observations about the situation in the country confirmed. The lucid -- the memorandum's lucid analysis of the situation and its clear message had a powerful effect on shaping public opinion. Overnight this document received huge popularity. It was mimeographed, passed from hand to hand, and sold on street corners." Now, you've denied that it was intentionally leaked, maintained that it was a secret document. I must ask you again: Was this document, perhaps like another famous document, Nacertanije in the 19th century, benefiting from its alleged secret nature, generating a particular interest in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to repeat what I've already stated and that is this: The document was not intended for the public at all. Now, the fact that it found itself in the public eye without the will of its authors is a coincidence, or it happened by chance that it was, but that it started to be mimeographed, some made a good business out of it, photocopying it and selling it even at marketplaces. The authors neither wished that nor are they responsible for that. But of course once it was already in the public, it had to have a ripple effect and influence the situation. But this was not the intention or will of its authors at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally on the text of the memorandum. Would you accept -- I don't have time to go over it, but would you accept that there are passages in the memorandum which are now reflected pretty well word-for-word in passages of your expert report to this Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is certainly quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly didn't copy out the memorandum, but I took part in its writing. So I haven't got two heads and two opinions about certain questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next point, time being so short. I'd like you, please, to comment on some passages from another chapter of Stambolic's book, yet to be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May it be distributed. This is -- this has been copied in both English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Chapter 7. The title can be seen, but that's not what I'm concerned about. I'm concerned at what we can find on page 13 in the English, and I'll get you the B/C/S page, please. Asked a question -- and this is on page 13 of the English and perhaps if there is a spare copy for the overhead projector, I'd be grateful. "Do you believe that you are being critical enough in measuring up your potential responsibility in our talks?" Because this book was a series of questions and answers. Gave an answer that included the following. Bottom of the page, please, Usher. "At any rate, by electing Milosevic President of the Presidency of the Central Committee, he was not elected any kind of leader; the leader would be created later. "A major role in the creation of the leader and building of the cult of the leader would be played by the intellectual elite in addition to the propaganda provided by the media. They composed and wrote songs about him; painters made his portraits and went to bow before him; his photos were copied in great numbers. Academicians started competing: Dobrica Cosic compared Milosevic to Nikola Pasic, Mihailo Markovic to Roosevelt, Milorad Ekmecic to de Gaulle, Milovan Danojlic to Karadjordje. Giving new meaning to Njegos, he wrote that Milosevic put 'new life into the Serbian soul.'" And if we could look, to save time, at another short passage on page 18 in the English, before I ask the question. On page 18: "He couldn't see --" this is the accused to whom Stambolic was referring: "He couldn't see or hear from anyone sensible or responsible that policies on other peoples had been pursued by having rallies in their squares or that policies on his own people had been conducted by using truncheons, water-guns, cold steel and firearms. Or that we had put knives under each other's throats and shouted at the top of our voice for dialogue at the same time. There was nothing in this country or its peoples that hopelessly divided them. By separating Serbs from everyone else, he divided them within. He divided them more dangerously than it appears." And then this: "Why was it necessary to incite Serbs outside Serbia in such an aggressive way to create new Serbian states instead of providing them with safe life and equal rights in their homeland of Herzegovina, Bosnia or Croatia? Haven't the Serbs suffered enough in the past?" With those two passages, first, is it right that this man, the accused, emerged as leader on the back of, in a sense, the intellectuals and what they had established through, for example, the thought processes lying within the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not of the same opinion as you. The appearance of Slobodan Milosevic meant something new in the political arena of Serbia, and the intelligentsia felt relief. Up until his arrival, there was something that was called verbal offence, that is to say intellectual restriction and censorship of the spoken word, the uttered word and phrase. So it meant an expansion of freedom. Slobodan Milosevic introduced the multi-party system in Serbia, for instance. So that was one step further towards democracy, a step that was seen as a progressive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is -- the question is, and I'll rephrase it to help you focus: This was not a man who led with his own ideas. He was a man who was needed by the ideas generated or expressed by the intellectuals through the memorandum, and he used or he instrumentalised those views by becoming leader and taking the thing forward, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You know what? It's like this: I said how within the circle of intellectuals they experienced his arrival, what they felt about it. Now, what the memorandum programme was is something else. There's a misunderstanding here. Slobodan Milosevic is certainly an intelligent man who was also well-versed in matters of the economy and politics so that his arrival --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he show any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute. May I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And certainly he stood out among the politicians of Serbia of the day with his own opinions. So he could have had a lot in common, not in an organised fashion but thoughts and thinking that coincided with analyses and observations set out in the memorandum. But this coincidence cannot be instrumentalised, if I can use the word, and construed as having been some sort of organisation. And let me say that there were very weak personal ties. So at the beginning when he first arrived and emerged, he included people like me in the commission and Academician Macura and several others working in the commission, but then that ceased. And many people later on -- many of these people later on joined the opposition or took the side of the opposition. So to look for ties and political ties, programme ties, are mere constructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And one programme tie we can establish is that he took over the issue of reforming the 1974 constitution from what was contained in the memorandum, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The initiative for a reform, and we didn't finish discussing the matter of the Blue Book, it was strong pressure from public opinion, and professional public opinion too. Today's Prime Minister, for example, the Prime Minister of Serbia, Mr. Kostunica, was sent away from the faculty as a result of the constitution, and that was in 1971. I will show you the annals of the faculty of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have so short a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And with Your Honours leave, I will have to defer my second question on that passage from Stambolic's book and move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You explain, Professor, that you and other academics and intellectuals associated with the memorandum became advisors to the accused. Now, in March 1991, there was the meeting between this accused and the late Franjo Tudjman. A lot of evidence we've heard suggesting that at that meeting what was discussed was the division of Bosnia. I asked you at the beginning whether you had been a member of the Serbian team set up after that initial meeting, a team consisting of yourself, Smilja Avramov, Ratko Markovic, and Zlatan Kukvlesic [phoen]. Were you a member of such a team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I would like to say that I was never appointed an advisor to President Milosevic. I was not appointed, I received no remuneration, but from time to time he consulted me on particular issues. This was simple consultation. It is true, however, that I was part of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not even know that previously there had been a meeting between President Milosevic and Tudjman, because we were given the task of meeting with a group from the Croatian side to consider the situation that had arisen in the Krajina, to see what the intentions were, because after the adoption of the Croatian constitution there was a very tense situation in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I ask you to deal very briefly with this. If you say you personally were never told anything about the original meeting. Did you, as we have heard from Smilja Avramov, in those meetings, the three meetings that happened in the hunting lodge close to Osijek on Dedinje in Belgrade and in Zagreb, did you deal with maps and such like that were consistent with planning the separation or division of Bosnia, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We did not deal with any maps at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When formulating his question, Mr. Nice said that there has been a lot of evidence here as to how Tudjman and I discussed the division of Bosnia. He is misleading the witness, because no evidence has been presented here that we discussed the division of Bosnia, nor could anyone expect such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... inappropriate interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just remind us of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I most certainly will. We have had evidence on the division of Bosnia coming from Paddy Ashdown. If you remember, there was a map that was drawn for him by the late President Tudjman. From Stipe Mesic, who was told by -- from Ante Markovic, who was told specifically by both sides of the division, and indeed the terms of the division. And I think from Hrvoje Sarinic as well, to name but four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think also -- I'm grateful. Also, Milan Babic covered it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So there we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you weren't engaged on work -- just see your answer. If you weren't engaged on work consistent with planning a division of Bosnia, what on earth were you doing for the three of you to meet on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First let me tell you, it would be difficult to define. We went without any instructions whatsoever. It consisted in getting information on what the other side's intentions were in the given situation. In the Krajina, this situation was such that it had a great impact on our discussions. They wanted Slobodan Milosevic to intervene because they failed to understand that they had a lot of independence. We had no possibilities or instructions in this respect. We were not authorised, and we had no contacts with Babic. These talks then meandered left and right. Bilandzic said that he had written an article about how the Serbs should be given autonomy and so on and so forth. There were even attempts, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to the summer of 1991, and two things happen in the summer of 1991, both of which you'll be familiar. First there was the Belgrade initiative which ended in November. You're acquainted with that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know anything about its content. I wasn't interested in it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But you know about it sufficiently for us to inform the Court through you that the Belgrade initiative was the accused's plan to retain within a former -- a reduced Yugoslavia, Serbia, Montenegro, and also Bosnia. Now, that was his plan at that stage, wasn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to The Hague, do you know about The Hague Conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you come to The Hague yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to The Hague to work on issues of succession and in the group for economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the head of the delegation for these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, can you assist us, please, with a new document that I'd like to be exhibited, recently provided by the relevant country, which is the country of which we are resident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be distributed and given a number if it's produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please, at paragraph 5. It would have to go on the overhead projector in English, I'm afraid. Paragraph 5. The document heading can be seen to refer to the conference between the 7th of September and the 5th of November. And paragraph 5 tells us that: "In the margins of the 4th plenary, a meeting was held on the 4th of October chaired by the minister for foreign affairs of the Netherlands," et cetera. "A statement was read out subsequently by the Netherlands minister at a press conference, reflecting the agreement of the Yugoslav parties involved after Minister van den Broek had obtained the acquiescence of all parties, Yugoslav parties at the plenary meeting. This included the principle that a political solution should be sought on the basis of the perspective of recognition of the independence of those republics in Yugoslavia wishing it. At the end of a negotiating process conducted in good faith and involving all parties, the recognition would be granted in the framework of a general settlement and have the following components: "A loose association or alliance of sovereign or independent republics; "Adequate arrangements to be made for the protection of minorities, including human rights guarantees and possibly special status for certain areas; "No unilateral changes in borders."
