Pausing there, Professor, you were here in The Hague, and you know that this accused agreed, as Lord Carrington has said, four times to this proposal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what he agreed to. He didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were here working for him and with him. Professor, did you not realise that all -- all but for the one thing that the accused was subsequently to do, the matter could have been settled in The Hague? Did you not appreciate that? Did you not appreciate that he'd consented at the beginning to the proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I was not fully acquainted with the political issues. Ms. Smilja Avramov was here as an advisor. I only attended a plenary session once with them. That was brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, just bear in mind the professor has said he was there to deal with economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 14, 16, 23, second paragraph of 23, again want of time, will help you. I note what you said, Professor, about not being involved in political issues, but we're going to come to the summer of 1992 as soon as I can get us there when you did indeed become involved, you may think, in political issues, but we'll look at that shortly. You know, of course, that eventually the accused declined The Hague proposal, didn't he, on the 18th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tell you, I did not deal with political issues. I was relatively little acquainted with the ongoing discussions on political issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, say no more. Professor, say no more. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to continue to press him on this? Because he said he did not come to The Hague to deal political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the professor has nevertheless volunteered a number of quite general opinions and I want to get the chronology before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall The Hague Conference and the Belgrade initiative, which was aimed at keeping Bosnia within a reduced form of Yugoslavia, all ended when the European Union asked the republics, in light of the failure of The Hague conference, if they were going to go for independence? Do you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've told you I'm not familiar with these details. I wasn't interested in the Belgrade initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't follow that course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you interested in the beginning of the following year in something called the Third Yugoslavia Convention, which was a convention of people from Serbia, Montenegro, and anywhere else who wanted to stay within Yugoslavia, a convention that brought forth people from various parts of Serbia and Montenegro but also from parts of Bosnia and Croatia? Were you aware of that convention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then in your role as an advisor, you featured -- you didn't feature, you took part in a body called the Council For Harmonisation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to have to show you some documents and see if we can remind you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never heard of A Council For Harmonisation. Harmonisation of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... state policy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of a commission for the economic reform of the Presidency of Serbia. I was a member of that. But this body ceased functioning in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 1991, I participated in the work of The Hague conference on economic issues and issues of succession and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think the Prosecutor wants to remind you of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would if I could adequately pronounce the Serbian title of the committee. [Serbian spoken] Does that make any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I didn't think it would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember sitting on a body, because we've got the stenographic notes of it, with Milan Panic, with this accused, with Dobrica Cosic, with Vladislav Jovanovic, and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I recall now. I recall very well. Now I know what you mean. This was a council --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... Dobrica Cosic, as the president or chairperson. I was not a member of the council, I only attended meetings twice because President Milosevic -- I think it was on two occasions only. I was not a member. The members were the presidents -- or, rather, the Prime Ministers of the republics and the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government. And on two occasions I was invited by President Milosevic to accompany him. And that was when the Vance-Owen Plan was being discussed. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the microphone of Professor Mihailovic was switched off when he was explaining that this was a council established by Dobrica Cosic, the then president of Yugoslavia. He explained its functioning. His microphone had been switched off, and I see it's not in the transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have just put it in, Mr. Milosevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to -- Professor, we have the stenographic notes of this series of meetings, all but two, which are not available to us at the moment, of the 9th of January, 1993, and the 21st of January, but you were present and you contributed to them, and I'm going to ask you for your assistance in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can they be -- the first one be placed on the overhead projector. 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may have confined yourself by choice to particular matters of economics, but you sat in very important political bodies, and here we see -- the usher -- we see the title in English, Shorthand Notes from the Session of the Council for Coordination of State Policy held on the 18th of August, 1992. Next page, please, and we see this, Milan Panic saying -- picking it up at page 18 of a very long document: "We're already in that position. The problem is that we have been accused for the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that we support the war in Bosnia, that we left the weapons for them to fight; that we support Karadzic financially. We spoke here about the ethnic cleansing. I heard from Dr. Brankovic that Serbs should get rid of others." To which the accused says: "Don't trouble us with your associates." Milan Panic continued: "He isn't my associate ..." Next paragraph, second or third sentence: "This afternoon I received the following information: Ethnic cleansing has begun. 15.000 Muslims from Sanski Most were given eight hours to leave their homes and make twenty kilometres to Jajce in order to reach the Muslims. This information was received from the United Nations. They asked me and said that I should stop it." Pause there. Do you remember, Professor, sitting in with this accused, with Milan Panic, with Dobrica Cosic, on meetings where ethnic cleansing, as alleged against Serbia, was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall attending this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice is referring to ethnic cleansing incited by Serbia. Where in the document does it say it was incited by Serbia? Who is he quoting? Who said it was incited by Serbia? He is construing a question. He is inventing it, in fact fabricating it. Panic is saying that he's being asked to stop something that's happening in Bosnia. Where does it say that Serbia instigated anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may make the correction, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I intervene here. I think the Prosecution should first of all establish whether this witness was present at a meeting before putting text like that, reading it out, getting it into the record, and then the witness says, Well, I wasn't at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Should we go to page 20? If the usher would be good enough to go to page 20. Here's a passage under the name --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? I remember that I attended meetings, and that's all that comes to my mind now, when the Vance-Owen Plan was being discussed. I know what I said and what President Milosevic said, and I remember, with reference to Panic, that once he made a statement at the airport in Moscow that he was abandoning continuity, and Belgrade was alarmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have your point. I have your point, Professor. Mr. Nice, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- if this examination to be fruitful, if the witness was not present, there's not much point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 20. If we go to page 20. The witness has acknowledged being present at two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if I could read to you what appears on page 20 of the English and then again we'll turn, in light of your answers, to page 45. At page 20 you said this -- you asked for the floor of the meeting and you said: "I just want to make a remark about introducing. With reference to the Conference on Yugoslavia, we were told we were not allowed to take part in the group of experts and other places on behalf of Yugoslavia because it's the Conference on Yugoslavia, which implies participation of six republics." Now, that's one contribution attributed to you. But if we go on beyond a long contribution from the accused, to page 45, and in mind your account of your limited interest, Milan Panic said: "And we the Serbs in Bosnia are 'naive.' They took 60 to 70 per cent of the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And you, Professor are recorded as contributing: "Let me explain this 70-30 per cent ratio. It is the result of historic conditions. Even after the World War II, the Serbs held the relative majority of the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Secondly, the Serbs were a discriminated nation, living on agriculture, whereas the Muslims lived in the cities and along the river valleys, and they were rather concentrated there. "These 60 per cent is factual land owned by the Serbs. This was not conquered in the war, it's factual ownership of the Serbs. "This is subject to speculations because people do not know the historic conditions." Now, some of that matches what's in your report, the condition of the Serbs, but despite your only being interested in economic issues, you seem to be pressing the suggestion that that large percentage of land should be retained. Do you remember making such a contribution, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say something to this effect but not as you interpreted it. My contribution was an historical and economic explanation, which is correct. The Muslims had a privileged position, and they lived in the towns and in river valleys, where the best land was, and the rest of the territory, the hills, belonged to others. That is how the situation arose that the Muslims were concentrated on a smaller -- in a smaller area and the Serbs in a broader area, and they became the owners of that land. It's a fact that Serbs owned over half the land in Bosnia. It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are scientific scholarly facts. But this has no other meaning. I was simply trying to explain how the land was distributed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move to a conclusion for this document. With the usher's assistance, just go to page 19. We've already seen, Professor, how there was discussion about ethnic cleansing, discussions about weapons left to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where we've seen that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... earlier. And on page 19, Milan Panic, at the bottom of that entry, is recording how he was taken aside by -- it says -- he refers to Mitterand, Boutros-Ghali, "Major takes me aside, everybody takes me aside and asks me these questions. I try to reply that I went to Sarajevo twice; all the time I am speaking about ethnic cleansing, and then I receive such a letter from the United Nations; we lose battles and we like to fight on the international scene, but we don't have ammunition. This is their ammunition. Then that one says aggressor, the Serbs are dreaming of their Greater Serbia, of the idea that the Serbs in Bosnia get rid of others and then join Serbia one day. That's what they say and they will be against us." And then one other short topic on page 38. The accused is recorded as saying: "As for the help provided to the Serbs in Bosnia, it is simply unacceptable for us to leave them helpless. This is not a war material, this is humanitarian aid - food, clothes, money. But we cannot deprive them of our assistance. I wonder, why would the assistance granted to the Muslims be humanitarian and they are getting weapons that have been apprehended in these conflicts, and our assistance is looked upon as military though our shipments do in the contain military supplies ..." Now, there you are. There's a couple of passages. Do you remember those things being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember at all. And as I said, I told you what I remember. There were two things that stand out: When the Vance-Owen Plan was being discussed and when Milan Panic, and you're mentioning Milan Panic now, when Milan Panic made a statement at the Moscow airport about the fact that he was relinquishing continuity and so on. And so that was a subject up for discussion at the council and the council decided to take a stand and insist upon continuity. Now, what Mitterand told Panic and what Panic told the council, I really don't remember any of that nor that there was any mention at all of any ethnic cleansing. Perhaps there was, but as I say, I don't remember. I was over 70 years old at the time when I went there, but I probably would have remarked on it had I heard that, because I do have some sort of continuous memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you more briefly, then, about the other meeting at which you were present, because you may be the only witness we ever have to explain the construct of these meetings and so on, but before I do and as an intervening -- not an intervening act, you recall a conference, an international conference on the former Yugoslavia that occurred in London on the 26th to the 28th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have, then, please, the next proposed exhibit, which is a document from Yugoslavia Through Documents From Its Creation to Its Dissolution. And if the usher would be good enough to take us in the English version to what is at the bottom right-hand corner page 711.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is a paper by the co-chairman setting out the position for Serbia and Montenegro, and I'll have to read the bullet points in full, Professor. "We welcome the fact that all participants to the conference have subscribed to the Statement on Bosnia and Herzegovina. All participants must fulfil the obligations to which they have agreed. In particular, Serbia and Montenegro face a clear choice. They have undertaken to: "Cease intervention across their borders with Bosnia and Croatia; "To the best of their ability restrain the Bosnian Serbs from taking territory by force and expelling the local population; "Restore in full the civil and constitutional rights of the inhabitants of Kosovo and Vojvodina and also ensure the civil rights of the inhabitants of the Sandjak; "Use their influence with the Bosnian Serbs to obtain the closure of their detention camps, to comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law and in particular the Geneva Conventions, and to permit the return of refugees to their homes. The Bosnian Croats and Muslims have given similar undertakings; "Fully observe the relevant resolutions of the United Nations Security Council; "Declare that they fully respect the integrity of present frontiers; "Guarantee the rights of ethnic and national communities and minorities within the borders of Serbia and Montenegro in accordance with the UN Charter, the CSCE and the draft convention of the EC Conference on Yugoslavia; "Work for the normalisation of the situation in Croatia, for implementation of the Vance Plan and for acceptance by the Serbs in the Krajina of special status as foreseen in the draft convention of the European Community Conference on Yugoslavia;" and then finally, "If, as suggested by Mr. Panic's recent letter to the president of the Security Council of the UN, Serbia and Montenegro do intend to fulfil these obligations in deed as well as word they will resume a respected position in the international community." Now, that's one of the things that followed from the London conference, and it set the terms upon which the former Yugoslavia could join the international community and indeed become a member of the UN, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These terms that I've read out to you were the terms imposed at this time by the London conference for Serbia, Montenegro, Yugoslavia, FRY, to rejoin the international community as a respected member. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one thing. I did not participate directly in the plenary session, although President Milosevic offered me to take part in the main hall. I was in the advisory body, not in the main hall, where different documents were passed around. Now, I know that there was a resolution on Montenegro on the last day when the conference was to end and that the then minister came to our delegation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you see, if you could have, please, displayed the Council For Harmonisation, or whatever it's properly described as, record for the 17th of September, which is the other one you attended at and where I want you to just help us a little bit, if you can, from memory, and I realise it's a long time ago. We see on page 65, at the bottom right-hand corner, the end of the passage that's been extracted -- the end of 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I see the name of the committee?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the name of the committee is differently expressed in this version or it may be translation. Council For Reconciliation Of The Standpoints Regarding State Politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I think, just to deal with that, this committee on which you sat was non-statutory, Professor? That would be correct, wouldn't it? It wasn't a statutory identified and designated committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it was outside the constitution. It was initiative taken by President Cosic, and that they were a body which wished to expand its competencies and authority in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we have this entry at the foot of 65 associated with you: "Mr. President, awhile ago --" and we can find it but I needn't trouble you with it: "Awhile ago I used the expression 'The King is dead, long live the King,' but the King needs to be murdered or to commit suicide." And then you went on to say: "As far as I can understand the things, the United Nations are facing the problem of expulsion of Yugoslavia from its membership and very serious legal and other problems. Of course, it is much simpler job for them - if Yugoslavia does it by itself." You said more, but can you remember discussing the issue to which the London conference requirements and membership of the United Nations connected? Can you remember discussing those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember them at all, and that doesn't -- those don't seem to be the kind of words I used. Are you sure that that comes under my name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure it comes under your name in the version that's been provided to us and the earlier -- if you have doubts, I'll take you back to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having spoken about that at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come back to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and if we come back to page 28 at the beginning of the extracted passage, you're in discussion with Miodrag Mitic, Ilija Djukic, and you responded to Djukic, who said: "Is it possible to let me say bridge this gap between the demise of one thing and the birth of the other exclusively within the realms of the United Nations Charter?" To which you replied: "I would like to pose a counter question - why this is all being done? If somebody wants to admit you, why do you have to cease to exist first? What is being interpolated then, what it stands, and then, The King is dead, long live the King, what dies with the King". Does that remind you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Let me say there was talk about membership, so maybe on certain occasions -- and I had a very clear-cut stand. If we're insisting upon continuity, then we can't ask for membership because Yugoslavia's membership -- Yugoslavia did not forfeit its membership in the United Nations, it was just suspended. So insistence upon continuity meant lifting the suspension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And agreement to seeking membership meant to give up on continuity, and that was a clear-cut stand. And I could not have had a different opinion at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, and just to give a little flavour of these meetings that may have to be considered carefully and in detail at a later stage, if you go to 62, it may be balance, but in any case I put it in to -- to assist and to encourage, perhaps, a general review of these documents. The accused, Professor, is recorded in this same meeting as saying the following: "Many others are creating serious problems. I think this has to be clarified --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The treatment of so-called ethnic cleansing. The statements have been given about how the ethnical cleansing will be prevented in Serbia. There is no ethnical cleansing in Serbia. There is no programme against ethnical cleansing, nor could it be because there is no ethnical cleansing. The deputy minister of the interior was replaced because he opposed the programme that does not exist..." and so on. Do you remember a discussion along those lines, or very approximately, in this meeting dealing with ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of any mention made of ethnic cleansing. It was the assessment made by journalists and people dealing with science connected to the ethnic cleansing in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that this was discussed, that ethnic cleansing was brought up in any official capacity in any official body, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I've used the opportunity of a witness who was present at the meetings to remind you of their existence. There's a series of them of which, as I said, two are missing, and they will at some stage have to be explored by the Prosecution, if by no one else, in some detail. Your Honours, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you plan to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood it that we have no time and that we have to close now. If you give me time, I do plan it. If you don't give me time, then I don't. So it's up to the physical feasibilities. But if there is time, I would like to see the documents that he's quoting from, because it appears that everything he's quoting from goes to our advantage. Of course there was no ethnic cleansing in Serbia ever, except in Kosovo, and that was exerted by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not time for you to comment now, but you couldn't resist the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is only one other topic that I'm going to deal with -- we have until ten past 12; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, until ten past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's only one other topic I have time to deal with, and that very briefly, Professor, and that's your economic evidence or your evidence about economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the Chamber, in our submission, this is of tangential, if any, relevance, and I'm going to deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One point in general: The notion, Professor, that Serbia is a victim of the oppression -- of the economic oppression of the other republics is one that doesn't fit comfortably, does it, with the reality that since the separation of the former republics of the former Yugoslavia, the divergence in economic performance between Serbia and Slovenia and Croatia has actually increased rather than decreased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't comment at all on trade between Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not trade between them but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what do you mean by the divergence has actually increased? Do you mean that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The per capita wealth, the performance of the economy measured to all international standards, the difference between Serbia and its former republic neighbours has increased over time rather than decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between Serbia and who?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course there was an increase. There was an increase even before, and especially afterwards, after the application of the sanctions. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's continued to this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on what you want to say by that. I said that there was a constant increase and that the trend carried on until the breakdown of Yugoslavia. The differences between Slovenia and Croatia on the one hand and Serbia on the other increased, the gulf increased to the detriment of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I can't take it further in the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have not in your report -- no, two things. First, you accept that your economic opinions as expressed in the memorandum haven't particularly changed because indeed they may well find expression in similar terms in your present expert report; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I wrote a book, Yugoslavia's Economic Reality, and of course I present my economic convictions in the book and in the memorandum as far as I took part in it. And I stand by my convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But what you have now before you is, I think, a document with which you will be familiar or of which you will know. That is it's an article by a highly respected and well-known economist, Ljubomir Madzar, or at least -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we go in the pages of the book to the top right-hand corner, page 179, we see in an article generally entitled Who Exploited Whom, we see reference to the SANU Memorandum, Expressions of Traumatisation in Economic Relations, and we see his expressions of opinion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this has to be the last question I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see that this expert reaches radically different conclusions, as you will know, Professor, from the economic conclusions of the memorandum itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the trait of a good economist to anticipate matters. I anticipated that you would bring this question up and ask your question and use this article. Let me say that the article contains only two tables, and they were borrowed tables, at that. And Mr. Madzar is a very good economist himself but he would have to settle accounts with himself because, and I can provide you with his text in Serbian written in 1989 in which he speaks quite differently on all these subjects, and he did so within the frameworks of a journal with a set political orientation, might I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: ... that document be exhibited. The position is that we remain of the view that the economic issue is marginal, if relevant at all. To have cross-examined this witness on matters of expertise would have taken far longer than the time available this morning at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we just deal with your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so we ask that this document be available to you for consideration on the economic issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We declined to admit tab 19 of this professor's binder. What's the difference with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one, first of all, it's a document that contains contrary opinions. He's acquainted with it. He hasn't referred to it in his own report, and he's now dealt with it, and it's very important, where we are so confined in time, that there is some material available to the contrary effect. I would, of course, if there had been more time available to deal with the witness who, as you now discover, could cover a very large amount of evidence because he was a fact witness on all sorts of things, I would have covered this, but it simply wasn't possible. And in our respectful submission, it would be entirely appropriate for his evidence to be -- not his evidence, his report to be before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did spend a fair bit of time, Mr. Nice, asking pretty pointless of questions of the witness rather than concentrating on this kind of thing, with all respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry you take that view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Especially when he made it clear he couldn't answer many of the questions that you tried to pose to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must, if I may respectfully say so, resist that observation. This is one of the only witnesses capable of dealing with these meetings, and if we wish to draw your attention the contents of those meetings, we have to give the witnesses available an opportunity to deal with them. We don't know if this accused is going to give evidence himself. We don't know if the only other person listed as somebody who can give evidence of these important meetings is going to be before us, and the alternative between asking questions of witnesses like this who were there, even if his memory is now faint, and not asking them at all is that it could be said to be unfair. So I respectfully differ from Your Honour's opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be an act of irresponsibility on the Chamber's part if we don't stop at the time, because the Appeals Chamber has to come in. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Our submission is none of these documents should go in. My biggest mistake, the massive section of text there, not a single bit of it was adopted in cross-examination. It just serves as a platform to get over the contrary views of another politician who is in opposition to the accused. It wasn't material or relevant to this witness, and the other documents that were put forward weren't adopted by him in any way, and we ask what relevance did they have to do with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we admitted Mr. Milosevic's documents on the basis of a reference, so I think parity would require that we do the same here. We don't have the time to deal with the exhibits now. We'll issue an order on that, as well as the four outstanding exhibits from the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Council for Harmonisation are, of course, already exhibits. They've already been exhibited by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in -- I must press the issue, if I get a chance to argue it, that these documents fall very squarely within the parameters being applied to the accused, and all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can just exhibit those -- the four from the previous -- yes, the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: From the previous witness, there were two maps. They will be marked as D267. The Cutileiro Plan will be D268. And the Vance-Owen Plan will be D269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have to adjourn on that basis, and I wish everybody a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask just one question, please? Well, if you've adjourned, never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very quickly. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Nice told you that in the delegation from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought it was a comment of an administrative nature, but I don't think we'll have to time to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just administrative, then. Just one administrative point. If you have accepted this article by Professor Madzar, where Mr. Nice strives to show that he had a differing opinion, then please accept professor articles -- Professor Madzar's article dating back to 1989 where Professor Mihailovic says that the same author has quite the opposite opinion in 1989, quite opposite to the opinion stated by Mr. Nice, and then you can see just how well-founded or not well-founded is his scientific thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will consider all these matters when we come to decide. We are adjourned until the 11th of January. Thank you, Professor, for coming to the International Tribunal and you may now leave. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.12 p.m.,
